title: Manitoba judge stays charge in 'rare' decision after Mountie failed to disclose relationship with key witness
summary: Drunk driving charges against a woman were stayed after an investigating RCMP officer appeared to have deliberately withheld information about his romantic relationship with a key witness, a Manitoba…

image.caption: Provincial court Judge Victoria Cornick stayed drunk driving charges against the woman in October. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

Drunk driving charges against a woman were stayed after an investigating RCMP officer appeared to have deliberately withheld information about his romantic relationship with a key witness, a Manitoba judge ruled.
Link was only discovered after Crown attorney's 'chance' run-in with couple

The officer's relationship with the witness came to light by fluke, when the Crown prosecutor in the case ran into the couple at a Canadian Tire, according to an October decision by provincial court Judge Victoria Cornick. That led to the woman withdrawing her guilty plea, and ultimately to a stay of proceedings because her Charter rights were violated.

"These decisions are rare. They are reserved for cases that are a clear problem, and I will say that I think this is a good example of something that falls squarely within that realm," the woman's lawyer, Matt Gould, told CBC News on Wednesday.

"In almost 20 years, I have not seen this behaviour from the police. It highlights how vulnerable we all are …, how much we rely on the assumption that the police are acting with integrity, that they are acting in a forthright manner, that they are being honest, that they aren't omitting critical facts."
RCMP were investigating a serious car crash outside of Flin Flon on March 4, 2023, Cornick wrote in her decision.
The woman was taken to hospital, where lead investigator Const. Christopher Chelmecki learned in an interview she might have been drinking alcohol, Cornick wrote.
Officers sought evidence that the woman had been drinking, but hospital personnel told them they would need a production order to access her medical records.
Matt Gould, seen here in a file photo, says it was 'chilling' how easy it would have been for the officer's omissions to have gone unnoticed. (CBC)
About a month later, another officer, Corp. Jordan Tost, told Chelmecki that two nurses at the Flin Flon hospital were potential witnesses and suggested that Chelmecki interview them.

The lead investigator followed through with Tost's request and interviewed the two nurses, who provided some evidence of alleged alcohol consumption, Cornick wrote. Those statements were sent to Tost, who filed a production order for the woman's medical records.
At no time during the investigation did Tost disclose he was in a romantic relationship with one of the nurses he told Chelmecki to interview, Cornick wrote.

blocks.text: Tost also initially said he didn't remember having a conversation with Chelmecki about interviewing the nurses, Cornick wrote, only to deny it altogether later on.
Gould said they challenged the methods police used to secure the woman's medical records in court, and a hearing was scheduled in July 2024 to challenge the validity of a warrant.
The defence requested Tost and the two nurses be cross-examined during the hearing, but the court only permitted Tost to take the stand.
Tost's relationship with the nurse was not disclosed in cross-examination during the hearing, and the production order was upheld, Cornick wrote.
The woman entered a guilty plea to driving with a blood alcohol concentration over the legal limit causing bodily harm — a plea that could have resulted in jail time, Cornick wrote.
Tost's relationship with the nurse wasn't disclosed until May 2025, Cornick wrote, when Crown prosecutor Kameron Hutchinson happened to run into the two at Canadian Tire.

Tost initially explained that "he did not consider the relationship relevant to the investigation," Cornick wrote, later stating he did not consider it at all. He also denied ever discussing the investigation with the nurse, the judge wrote.
The woman was permitted to withdraw her guilty plea last January.
One RCMP officer told another there were two nurses at the Flin Flon hospital who were potential witnesses. (Eric Westhaver/CBC)

Cornick wrote that while there is no evidence to suggest the nurse provided inaccurate or fabricated information, the omission prevented the justice who authorized the production order from making a fully informed decision.

"Disclosure of the relationship would have permitted scrutiny of how [the nurse] came to be identified as a witness, what Cpl. Tost knew about her potential evidence before the interview, and whether any relevant communications or qualifications were absent from the account presented to the authorizing justice," Cornick wrote.
The deliberate omission also compromised the July 2024 hearing, the judge wrote, as the court denied the defence's request to cross-examine the two nurses.
"It is unnecessary to find that full disclosure would have defeated the production order with certainty," Cornick wrote. "What is clear is that the review process was subverted in a substantive way."
Cornick also raised concerns the omission was never disclosed deliberately, adding the process "cannot rely on chance public encounters as safeguards against miscarriages of justice."
There are no rules against evidence coming from an officer's significant other, Gould wrote, noting that was never the main focus of the case.

"The concern was the lack of clarity, the omission of that information, the recognition by the court that that information was not provided," she wrote. "The information did not make it to the court and it absolutely should have."

While the public deserves to see justice for the alleged criminal conduct, which left a victim suffering life-altering injuries, Cornick said protecting the fairness and integrity of the justice system is more important.
Like Cornick, Gould said the information about the relationship coming to light by pure happenstance is concerning.

"It's not insignificant. The jeopardy faced here is very easily years in jail," Gould said. "It's critical that the system operates appropriately, and it's terrifying. It should be chilling to anybody to understand how easy it would have been for this to have gone unnoticed."
The lawyer said he hopes this decision will prevent abuse of power from occurring in the future.
"There will be real consequences for the officer, in my opinion, and the RCMP," Gould said. "The impact on this officer's credibility cannot be understated."
